extracted.intended_audience: state environmental agencies, EPA rulewriters, regulated electric utility steam generating unit owners/operators, and stakeholders participating in notice-and-comment
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble-level regulatory guidance and criteria defining applicability, subcategories, and the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for existing fossil fuel-fired electric utility steam generating units under CAA section 111.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designated facility applicability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A designated facility is any fossil fuel-fired electric utility steam generating unit (i.e., utility boiler or IGCC unit) that: (1) was in operation or had commenced construction on or before January 8, 2014; (2) serves a generator capable of selling greater than 25 MW to a utility power distribution system; and (3) has a base load rating greater than 260 GJ/h (250 million British thermal units per hour (MMBtu/h)) heat input of fossil fuel (either alone or in combination with any other fuel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with implementing regulations and prior CAA section 111 rulemakings (e.g., 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTT). For the emission guidelines the term refers to a single EGU affected by the guidelines and is used throughout the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existing vs. new/reconstructed/modified source dates
rubrics_metrics.description: The emission guidelines do not apply to any steam generating units that are new after January 8, 2014, or reconstructed after June 18, 2014. A coal-fired steam generating unit that undertakes a modification after the proposal publication date (May 23, 2023) and is treated as a 'new' source under revised standards of performance would not be subject to these emission guidelines; modifications prior to that date would be treated as existing sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretation follows CAA section 111(a)(6) and aligns applicability with dates used in 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTT. The timing of modifications/reconstructions determines whether a unit remains covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions from requirement to establish standards under a state plan (enumerated list)
rubrics_metrics.description: EGUs that may be excluded from the requirement to establish standards under a state plan include: (1) units subject to 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTT as a result of commencing a qualifying modification or reconstruction; (2) steam generating units subject to a federally enforceable permit limiting net-electric sales to one-third or less of potential output or ≤219,000 MWh annually and annual net-electric sales have never exceeded that limit; (3) non-fossil fuel units (capable of deriving ≥50% heat input from non-fossil fuel at base load) subject to a permit limiting fossil fuel use to ≤10% of annual capacity factor; (4) CHP units subject to a permit limiting annual net-electric sales to no more than either 219,000 MWh or the product of the design efficiency and the potential electric output; (5) units that serve a generator along with other affected EGUs where the effective generation capacity is ≤25 MW; (6) municipal waste combustor units subject to 40 CFR part 60, subpart Eb; (7) commercial or industrial solid waste incineration units subject to 40 CFR part 60, subpart CCCC; (8) EGUs that derive >50% of heat input from an industrial process that does not produce any electrical or mechanical output or useful thermal output used outside the affected EGU; (9) coal-fired steam generating units that have elected to permanently cease operation prior to January 1, 2032.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many of these exemptions mirror existing provisions in 40 CFR 60.5509(b) and rationale provided in section VIII.E.1 of the preamble. Some exemptions correspond to finalized revisions in other subparts; states should apply these consistently with those regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption for coal-fired units permanently ceasing operation before January 1, 2032
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing coal-fired steam generating EGUs that have elected to cease operating before January 1, 2032, are not regulated by these emission guidelines; the exemption applies until the earlier of December 31, 2031, or the date the source demonstrates in the state plan that it plans to cease operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: such sources have limited emission reduction potential and capital-intensive controls (e.g., CCS or co‑firing) are unlikely to be cost-reasonable given a very short amortization period. If a source continues operating past the date, it is no longer exempt; states should address exempted sources in plans per section X.E.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic (non-contiguous) applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is not finalizing emission guidelines for existing steam generating units in states and territories outside of the contiguous U.S. (including Alaska, Hawaii, Guam, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands) at this time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: modeling supporting the final guidelines focuses on the contiguous U.S.; few, if any, coal-fired units meet applicability criteria outside the contiguous states; proposed BSERs for non‑continental oil-fired units would have yielded few reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of IGCC units
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing IGCC units are included in the subcategory of coal-fired steam generating units; BSERs for coal-fired steam generating units (co‑firing for medium-term and CCS for long-term units) apply to IGCC units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: IGCC units gasify coal/solid fossil fuel to syngas and may be suitable for pre-combustion capture; CO2 concentrations post-water-gas shift are high and both pre-combustion and post-combustion capture approaches may apply. EPA is not distinguishing IGCC from other coal-fired EGUs for BSER purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coal/oil/natural gas fuel‑type subcategory definitions (thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fuel-type subcategory definitions are finalized based on the type and amount of fossil fuel used after December 31, 2029: - Coal-fired unit: burns coal for >10.0% of the average annual heat input during any continuous 3-calendar-year period after Dec 31, 2029, or >15.0% of annual heat input during any one calendar year after Dec 31, 2029, or retains capability to fire coal after Dec 31, 2029. - Oil-fired unit: not a coal-fired unit, no longer retains capability to fire coal after Dec 31, 2029, and burns oil >10.0% of average annual heat input during any continuous 3-year period after Dec 31, 2029, or >15.0% in any one calendar year after Dec 31, 2029. - Natural gas-fired unit: not coal- or oil-fired, no longer retains capability to fire coal after Dec 31, 2029, and burns natural gas >10.0% of average annual heat input during any continuous 3-year period after Dec 31, 2029, or >15.0% in any one calendar year after Dec 31, 2029.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions are finalized to reflect the state of the source on the compliance date of January 1, 2030 and thereafter, to avoid perverse incentives for delayed conversion. Retaining the capability to fire coal after Dec 31, 2029 affects categorization; states may use RULOF provisions to particularize standards for conversions or transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and non-rolling determination of fuel-type subcategorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Fuel type subcategorization is based on the state of the source on the compliance date of January 1, 2030, and during any period thereafter; EPA is not adopting a continually rolling fuel-type determination that would update after the initial compliance date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: constraints on timing prevent a perverse incentive to defer conversions in a way that undermines emissions reductions. If a source cannot fully convert to natural gas by Jan 1, 2030 it will be treated as coal-fired, although states may use RULOF to particularize standards. If a state relies on operating conditions within the control of the source as the basis for less stringent standard or longer compliance schedule, those conditions must be included as enforceable requirements in the state plan (40 CFR 60.24a(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Final BSER for long-term coal-fired steam generating units (CCS at 90% capture)
rubrics_metrics.description: For long-term coal-fired steam generating units, EPA is finalizing CCS with 90 percent capture of CO2 at the stack as the BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: CCS achieves substantial unit-level emissions reductions (far greater than 40% co‑firing or partial CCS), is adequately demonstrated at scale, is widely applicable, sequestration opportunities exist nationwide, and costs are reasonable considering recent declines and incentives (e.g., IRC section 45Q). EPA finalized a compliance date of January 1, 2032 for CCS-based standards and will apply CCS-based standards only to units that plan to operate at least seven years after the compliance date (i.e., beyond Jan 1, 2039) given amortization/cost considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final BSER for medium-term coal-fired steam generating units (40% natural gas co‑firing)
rubrics_metrics.description: For medium-term coal-fired steam generating units (those demonstrating they plan to permanently cease operating by Jan 1, 2039), EPA is finalizing natural gas co‑firing at 40 percent of heat input as the BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA finalized a compliance date of January 1, 2030 for the co‑firing BSER. Rationale: co‑firing entails substantially less up-front infrastructure and capital expenditure than CCS and is cost-reasonable for many units that can amortize costs over the relevant period (EPA assumed amortization up to 9 years for units operating after Jan 1, 2030 and through 2039).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of partial-CCS (lower capture rates) and HRI as BSER for long-term units
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is not finalizing partial-CCS at lower capture rates (e.g., 30 percent) or Heat Rate Improvement (HRI) as the BSER for long-term coal-fired units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: partial-CCS achieves substantially fewer unit-level reductions and can be higher cost on a per-ton basis; CCS at 90% is achievable and more effective. HRI provides limited reductions and risks rebound effects. The IRC section 45Q tax credit may not apply to partial CCS, reducing its cost-effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-reasonableness metrics and amortization period considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA used cost-reasonableness metrics of $18.50 per MWh of generation and $98 per ton of CO2 reduced to evaluate controls. CCS was determined cost-reasonable for units that can amortize capital costs over more than 7 years (i.e., operate past Jan 1, 2039); natural gas co‑firing at 40% meets metrics for many units with amortization periods of more than 2 years (operate after Jan 1, 2032).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA evaluated costs across amortization periods: for very short amortization (e.g., retirement by Jan 1, 2032 with <2 years), CCS and 40% co‑firing often exceed EPA's cost metrics. EPA provides population statistics (e.g., with 1‑year amortization only ~1% of units can co‑fire 40% at costs below both metrics; with 2‑year amortization ~18% can co‑fire 40% below metrics; ~50% can co‑fire 20% below metrics). States may use RULOF where particular sources have fundamentally different costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination that CCS is adequately demonstrated (capture, transport, sequestration)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA determines CCS is adequately demonstrated: all components—CO2 capture, transport, and sequestration—have been demonstrated concurrently and in industrial/commercial applications, and CO2 capture at ~90% has been demonstrated on coal-fired units (e.g., Boundary Dam Unit 3); numerous U.S. and international projects and pipelines provide precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence cited includes long-running industrial solvent-based capture, operating CCS projects (e.g., Shute Creek, Great Plains Synfuels), commercial coal CCS demonstrations (Boundary Dam, Petra Nova), tens of millions of tons stored underground, and wide availability of sequestration reservoirs. PHMSA pipeline safety regulations cover transport.

rubrics_metrics.name: CO2 capture technical description and process components
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-combustion CO2 capture typically uses liquid solvents (commonly amine-based) in CO2 scrubbers: flue gas is absorbed by solvent, solvent regenerated by heating to release CO2, CO2 is compressed and transported (usually by pipeline) for geologic sequestration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technical explanation supports determinations of feasibility and adequate demonstration; EPA notes available minor technological improvements and solvent developments claim capture rates ≥95% for modern capture plants.

rubrics_metrics.name: RULOF (reasonably likely to be used or feasible) procedural provision for particularizing standards
rubrics_metrics.description: If a particular source has costs of a BSER that are fundamentally different from EPA's fleet-average assumptions, the state may consider the source a candidate for a different control requirement under the RULOF provision; if a state relies on operating conditions within the control of the source to provide a less stringent standard or longer compliance schedule, it must include those operating conditions as an enforceable requirement in the state plan (40 CFR 60.24a(g)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides states a mechanism to particularize standards for individual units based on special circumstances (e.g., atypical costs or capabilities), but requires enforceable plan elements and documentation per the preamble discussion.
